identification.summary: Cadet Blizzard is a Russian state actor that Microsoft associates with the GRU. Microsoft began tracking it as DEV-0586 in January 2022, after the WhisperGate destructive malware and defacements of Ukrainian government websites [S1][S2]. Microsoft says its goals are disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation. Its main targets are Ukrainian government organizations and IT service providers, with further targets in Europe, Central Asia and Latin America [S1]. US government agencies attribute WhisperGate and later operations against NATO members to GRU Unit 29155 [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft assesses the group has been operational in some capacity since at least 2020, with historical compromises of Eastern European entities as early as April 2021 [S1]. WhisperGate first appeared on victim systems on 2022-01-13 [S2]. The US joint advisory says Unit 29155 has conducted offensive cyber operations since at least 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cadet Blizzard (formerly DEV-0586; renamed in April 2023) [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as distinct from the other GRU-affiliated groups Forest Blizzard (STRONTIUM) and Seashell Blizzard (IRIDIUM) [S1]. MITRE tracks it as Ember Bear (G1003) with aliases UNC2589, Bleeding Bear, DEV-0586, Cadet Blizzard, Frozenvista and UAC-0056 [S7]. The joint advisory maps Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear, Frozenvista, UNC2589 and UAC-0056 to Unit 29155 activity, and cautions that these may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: MITRE tracks Saint Bear (G1031; Storm-0587, TA471, UAC-0056, Lorec53) separately. It is the Saint Bot/OutSteel phishing cluster, and MITRE says it is distinct from Ember Bear despite past confusion [S7][S8]. Microsoft reports that Cadet Blizzard has intersected with Storm-0587, a phishing and document-stealer cluster active since April 2021, but tracks it separately [S1]. This profile therefore does not merge Saint Bot or OutSteel campaign facts into Cadet Blizzard.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: the GRU (Main Directorate of the General Staff). Microsoft assesses the actor is associated with the GRU [S1]. The FBI, NSA and CISA attribute the corresponding cyber activity to GRU Unit 29155 [S3], and a US indictment names a Unit 29155 cyber commander and officers [S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft says it has 'gained high confidence in our analysis and knowledge of the actor's tooling, victimology, and motivation' and assesses that Cadet Blizzard is associated with the GRU [S1]. The September 2024 joint advisory makes a US and allied government attribution to GRU Unit 29155. It also notes that vendor alias mappings may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. US federal indictments (June 2024 and September 2024) charge a civilian and five GRU officers over WhisperGate. These charges are allegations, not convictions [S4][S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response [S1][S2]; FBI/NSA/CISA joint advisory AA24-249A [S3]; DOJ indictments of Amin Stigal (June 2024) and of Col. Yuriy Denisov and four Unit 29155 lieutenants (September 2024) [S4][S5]. Microsoft also assesses that at least one Russian private-sector organization materially supported the WhisperGate operation [S1]. The FBI assesses that the cyber operators are junior active-duty GRU officers working under experienced unit leadership, and that they rely in part on non-GRU cybercriminals [S3].

objectives: Microsoft lists disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation, and notes that some operations appear designed as public signals [S1]. The US advisory says Unit 29155 conducts computer network operations against global targets for espionage, sabotage and reputational harm [S3][S4]. It exposes stolen data through hack-and-leak fronts such as 'Free Civilian' [S1].

regions: Europe and NATO member states, especially those providing military aid to Ukraine [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft describes a 'compromise one, compromise many' approach through IT providers [S1]. The FBI observed more than 14,000 instances of domain scanning across 26 NATO members and several other EU countries (reported via secondary coverage of the advisory) [S3]. The Stigal indictment says later targets included systems in countries supporting Ukraine, including the United States [S5].

capabilities.summary: Destructive capability: WhisperGate is a two-stage wiper disguised as ransomware. It overwrites the Master Boot Record with a fake ransom note, then downloads a file corrupter from Discord that overwrites targeted files, and it has no recovery mechanism [S2]. Initial access comes mainly through exploitation of internet-facing web servers and of known Confluence and Exchange vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-26084, CVE-2022-41040 and ProxyShell [S1]. Post-exploitation relies on web shells, renamed open-source and living-off-the-land tools (Impacket, netcat, GOST, procdump), and anonymization through commercial VPNs and Tor. Microsoft also reports anti-forensics and disabling of Microsoft Defender [S1][S2]. Operations are paired with website defacement and hack-and-leak information operations [S1]. Microsoft judges the group less prolific than Seashell Blizzard and its operational security weaker than that of Forest Blizzard or Seashell Blizzard [S1].

campaigns.name: Early compromises of Eastern European entities
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports historical Cadet Blizzard compromises of Eastern European entities as early as April 2021.

campaigns.name: WhisperGate destructive attacks on Ukraine
campaigns.summary: Destructive MBR wiper and file corrupter disguised as ransomware hit dozens of systems at Ukrainian government, non-profit and IT organizations, about a month before the February 2022 invasion.

campaigns.name: Ukrainian government website defacements and 'Free Civilian' leak site
campaigns.summary: Defacements of Ukrainian institutions' websites came alongside a Tor-hosted 'Free Civilian' hack-and-leak front that published data stolen from Ukrainian organizations.

campaigns.name: Peak operational tempo
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says Cadet Blizzard activity peaked between January and June 2022, then declined.

campaigns.name: Re-emergence and Free Civilian Telegram channel
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed the group re-emerge in January 2023. In February 2023, Free Civilian moved to a Telegram channel to leak data.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public naming as Cadet Blizzard
campaigns.summary: Microsoft promoted DEV-0586 to the named actor Cadet Blizzard, associated it with the GRU, and described it as distinct from Forest Blizzard and Seashell Blizzard.

campaigns.name: DOJ indictment of Amin Stigal
campaigns.summary: US charges Russian national Amin Stigal with conspiring with the GRU to destroy Ukrainian government systems in the WhisperGate campaign; the State Department offers a reward of up to $10M.

campaigns.name: Joint advisory AA24-249A and indictment of five Unit 29155 officers
campaigns.summary: FBI, NSA, CISA and partners attribute the activity to GRU Unit 29155. A superseding indictment charges Col. Yuriy Denisov and four lieutenants over WhisperGate and related hacking; combined rewards total $60M.

diamond.adversary: GRU-associated Russian operators (Microsoft) [S1]. US government attribution is to GRU Unit 29155, reportedly junior active-duty officers under experienced leadership, aided by a civilian co-conspirator and non-GRU cybercriminals [S3][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: WhisperGate MBR wiper and file corrupter [S2]; exploitation of Confluence and Exchange vulnerabilities; web shells; Impacket, netcat, GOST and procdump; anti-forensics [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Commercial VPNs (IVPN, SurfShark) and Tor for anonymization; Discord for hosting second-stage payloads; Tor and Telegram hack-and-leak channels ('Free Civilian') [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government, IT providers, NGOs, law enforcement and emergency services. Beyond Ukraine: European and NATO states, Central Asia, Latin America and US systems [S1][S2][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Support to Russia's war against Ukraine. Pre-invasion destructive signalling, intimidation, and pressure on states that support Ukraine [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers, Confluence and Exchange on network perimeters and DMZs, trust relationships with IT service providers, and Windows MBR and file systems [S1][S2].

gaps: The primary text of CISA advisory AA24-249A (cisa.gov) and the DOJ press releases (justice.gov) could not be opened because the hosts are blocked. Their content here comes from search-result summaries and press coverage [S3][S4][S5].
The MITRE ATT&CK G1003 and G1031 pages could not be fetched. Their descriptions come from search-result summaries [S7][S8].
The CrowdStrike 'Who is EMBER BEAR' blog and the Symantec Nodaria report (both in the imported references) could not be fetched, so their claims are not used.

Cluster boundary unresolved: UAC-0056 is listed under both MITRE Ember Bear and Saint Bear. MITRE's Saint Bot software entry associates the tool with Ember Bear, while its Saint Bear group entry calls the two clusters distinct [S7][S8]. Unit 42 attributes Saint Bot and OutSteel phishing (for example against a Ukrainian energy organization on 2022-02-01) to UAC-0056, which other vendors call TA471, SaintBear and Lorec53 [S6]. The imported record's aliases (Saint Bear, SaintBear, Lorec53, TA471, Nodaria, Storm-0587, DEV-0587) may belong to the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster rather than to Cadet Blizzard and should be reviewed.
The imported record's software list includes Saint Bot, which may belong to Saint Bear/Storm-0587 rather than Cadet Blizzard [S8].
No public Microsoft reporting on Cadet Blizzard after 2023 was found in this research pass, so current activity levels are unverified.
The identity of the Russian private-sector organization that Microsoft says supported WhisperGate is not public in the sources reviewed [S1].
The full list of CVEs and initial-access techniques in AA24-249A was not reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing web servers and Confluence and Exchange instances on perimeters and in DMZs, plus IT service providers whose access reaches many government customers [S1]. The operating environment covers Ukraine and the NATO states that support it, including US systems [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Destructive wipers can make government and NGO endpoints inoperable without recovery [S2]. Hack-and-leak and defacement add information effects aimed at intimidation and reputational harm [S1][S3]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit a public-facing service, then plant a web shell, dump credentials (LSASS, registry hives), move laterally with Impacket, and either exfiltrate data and leak it or deploy a wiper; anonymization runs through VPNs and Tor [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage and hack-and-leak against Ukrainian and allied government and IT-provider networks, preceded by broad scanning of NATO domains [S1][S3]. MDCOA is coordinated destructive wiper deployment through compromised IT providers against allied government or critical-infrastructure networks during a crisis [S1][S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: scanning spikes against exposed Confluence and Exchange servers; new web shells on DMZ servers; renamed procdump, netcat or GOST binaries; reg save of SAM or SYSTEM hives; Impacket remote execution over ADMIN$; payloads retrieved from Discord; disabled Defender; new Free Civilian-style leak channels [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear and Unit 29155 reporting together, but keep the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster separate to avoid mis-cueing defenders [S1][S3][S7][S8]. Authorities: US attribution rests on the joint advisory and indictments. Vendor alias mappings are flagged as inexact, so planners should cite the government attribution for actions and vendor reporting for TTPs [S3][S4]. Mission assurance: give priority to patching and monitoring internet-facing collaboration and mail servers, and to backups and MBR protection for mission systems that depend on IT service providers, given the 'compromise one, compromise many' approach and the destructive intent [S1][S2]. Coordination: because targeting includes allies that support Ukraine and the US, coordinate with CISA, FBI and allied CERTs (for example CERT-UA) on indicators and on hack-and-leak responses [S1][S3][S5].
